extracted.intended_audience: general readers, bibliophiles, book designers, and printers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on aesthetic choices in book production (decoration, illustrations, margins, edges, typography) and prescriptive recommendations for serious reading practice (what to read, how to read, reading attitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of color judged by propriety and result
rubrics_metrics.description: It is all a question of propriety, literary and artistic. The beauty of the result and never the beauty of the means by itself must be the test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color (initials, rubrication, colored headings, lines, paragraphs) should be employed only when it contributes to the overall beauty and propriety of the book; do not add color merely for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations must be fit and compatible with type
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that an engraving is beautiful is no proof that it will contribute beauty to a book; it may only make an esthetic mess of the text and itself. As types are composed of firm black lines, only fairly strong black-line engravings have any artistic right in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match illustration style and strength to the typographic text; avoid delicate engravings that clash with type. Diagrams, being lines, can sometimes be more decorative than pictorial illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of pictorial plates from text when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: White-line engravings and half-tones may be allowed if they are printed apart from the text and separated from it, either by being placed at the end of the book or by having a sheet of opaque paper dividing each from the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If illustrations (white-line engravings, half-tones, or plates) cannot harmonize with the text page, print them on separate sheets or collect them apart; ensure the legend faces the picture so the reader need not look beyond the two pages when viewing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legend placement for pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: The legend of the picture should face it so that the reader will have no occasion to look beyond the two pages when he has them before him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always place the caption/legend opposite the illustration to avoid forcing the reader to flip pages; improves usability of separated plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margins and untrimmed edges preserve design integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the book is designed correctly from the beginning, the margins will be of just the right width and the edges cannot be trimmed without making them too narrow. Besides, the untrimmed edges are witnesses to the integrity of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not trim margins that were designed to be that width; consider top-edge gilding only sparingly (for beauty and dust protection) and prefer shaving rather than trimming to avoid visibly reducing margins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edge decoration — limited appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: The gilding of all the edges, or 'full gilt,' is hardly appropriate to the book beautiful, though it may be allowed in devotional books... Edges may be goffered... though the result... is more curious than ornamental. The edges may even be made to receive pictures, but here again the effect smacks of the barbaric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve full gilt and extreme edge ornamentation for special contexts (e.g., devotional books); avoid goffering or pictorial edges for ordinary books as they tend toward curiosity or barbaric effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness is the sole limit on ornament and illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: As in the use of other ornamental features, there are no bounds to the use of illustration except that of fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the requirement of fitness (appropriateness to text and purpose) govern all ornamentation decisions rather than arbitrary taste or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic minutiae and material choices are interdependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Every phase of the subject bristles with moot points... the proper shape for the dot of the i; the size of the dot and its place above the letter... the question of laid or wove paper, nor of the intermixture of different series or sizes of types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that small typographic choices (dot shapes, paper type, mixing type sizes) are numerous and interrelated; settle them deliberately because one decision may determine many others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's informed appreciation promotes better books
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing that the true artist craves so much... as understanding of his work and the welcome that awaits his work in hand from the lips of 'those who know.' Thus those who appreciate and welcome the book beautiful, by their encouragement help to make it more beautiful... they discourage ugliness in books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate informed, appreciative criticism rather than uninformed cocksure criticism; public taste and patronage influence producers toward excellence and away from ugliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading great books as a duty to oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: As a duty to ourselves, we must make the acquaintance of the books that the common judgment of the world has pronounced to be of the most value. They must become more than names to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reading canonical works as self-improvement and a moral/intellectual duty; seek acquaintance with those books judged of most lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic reading — read by authors and groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reading is far more profitable than desultory reading... One excellent way to achieve system is to read by authors—to make the author a study, in his writings and his life... read not merely separate authors, but of a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt organized reading plans: study an author's life alongside chronological reading of his works; consider reading coherent groups (e.g., Elizabethans, New England group) to gain contextual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study author biographies and chronological reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Read his life in Mrs. Field's brief Beacon Biography, dipping at the same time into his 'Note-Books,' and then read some of his short stories and the 'Scarlet Letter.' ... read each author's writings in chronological succession; so they will stand in orderly relation with his life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use biographies and notebooks for context; read an author's works in chronological order to relate them to his life and intellectual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct reading of primary text over commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: The general reader should clearly distinguish between the two kinds of commentary... Surely it is the thought of Shakespeare that we want, and not the pedantry of minute scholarship... reading about Shakespeare is not reading Shakespeare; that means, for the time at least, self-surrender to Shakespeare's leading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize reading the primary author before diving into textual or scholarly notes; use commentary selectively for guidance but not as a substitute for direct engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance reading contemporaries with the masters
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall, of course, read our contemporaries, and we have a right to, so long as we do not give them the time and attention that clearly belong to their betters... the near carries with it an appearance of importance that is an illusion... 'back number.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read contemporary writers but guard against letting them displace time better spent on enduring masterpieces; be wary of periodical fashions and transient voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading attitude: humility, gratitude, and self-surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: This is the spirit of a joyous but devoutly grateful expectance... The gratitude I surely owe the author... it is only in the humility born of such an attitude that I can make a complete approach to my author and gain that uplift and enrichment of the soul, which—and not pastime nor pleasure—is the true end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach great books with a devotional humility and gratitude; aim for spiritual/enlightening uplift rather than mere amusement.
